kjv: that lay on forty five pillars, fifteen in a row
mine: above the beams that rested on the pillars, forty-five of them, fifteen to a row
note: The number forty-five follows hatsela'ot (beams/side rooms) "that were on the pillars"; the KJV attaches it to the pillars, which conflicts with the four rows of pillars in v. 2.
Hebrew 'av is obscure here; it is usually taken as an overhang or canopy rather than a single thick beam.

kjv: had another court within the porch
mine: in the other court set back from the hall
note: Hebrew hatser ha'aheret mibbeit la'ulam locates the king's residence in a separate court behind the hall, not a court inside the porch.
Hebrew nehoshet is copper or bronze (copper-tin); brass (copper-zinc) was not used in Solomon's day. The same applies throughout the chapter and book.

kjv: did compass either of them about
note: The Hebrew says the line went around "the second pillar" (ha'ammud hasheni), an elliptical way of giving the same measure for each; the KJV smooths it.

kjv: to cover the chapiters that were upon the top, with pomegranates
mine: two rows of pomegranates ... to cover the capitals that were on top of the pillars
note: The MT appears to have exchanged "pillars" and "pomegranates" (it reads "the capitals on top of the pomegranates"); I follow the widely accepted transposition, while the KJV rearranges the words to make sense of the MT.
Hebrew peqa'im are gourd-shaped ornaments; "knops" (knobs) is archaic and vague.

kjv: upon the ledges there was a base above
mine: on the frames as well, above
note: Hebrew ken here is the adverb "likewise," not the noun ken "base"; the KJV read it as the noun.

kjv: certain additions made of thin work
note: Hebrew loyot ma'aseh morad are wreaths or garlands in hanging (pendant) work.

kjv: plates of brass: and the four corners thereof
mine: bronze axles, and its four feet
note: Hebrew sarne are axles (cf. v. 32 in sense) and pa'amotav its feet, not plates and corners.

kjv: according to the proportion of every one
note: Hebrew kema'ar ish means "according to the clear space of each," i.e. wherever there was room.
Hebrew devir is the innermost room of the temple; "oracle" now suggests a prophetic utterance.
